title: Hairpin lace scarf
subtitle: A long classic scarf worked on a hairpin lace frame with a joining row.
excerpt: Hairpin lace produces long strips of looped fabric on a U-shaped frame. This scarf joins two strips side by side with a simple crochet joining row for a lightweight, loopy texture in fingering weight yarn.
sourceNotes: Hairpin lace as a domestic crochet technique dates to the late 19th century, documented in Weldon's Practical Needlework and similar British publications. The two-strip scarf format is a standard beginner project. This layout and joining method are original to Homemade.

glossaryTerms.definition: A crochet technique where yarn is looped around a U-shaped metal frame while a central chain is worked with a hook, producing a strip of looped fabric on each side.
A U-shaped metal or plastic tool with two parallel prongs held apart by a connector bar. The spacing of the prongs sets the width of the lace strip.
A crochet row that links the loops from two hairpin lace strips together, creating a flat seam down the centre of the piece.

crochet.gaugeText: One hairpin lace strip on a 5 cm wide frame: 20 loops per 10 cm of strip length in fingering weight.
crochet.finishedSizeText: Scarf approximately 18 cm wide x 160 cm long.

content.text: This scarf is made of two
strips joined along their inner edges. Each strip is worked on a
set 5 cm wide. The outer loops are left free, giving the scarf its loopy, airy texture.

Set the frame to 5 cm. Make a slip knot and loop it onto the left prong. Bring the yarn around the right prong and work 1 double crochet through the central loop. Rotate the frame, wrapping yarn around the back prong. Work 1 double crochet through the new central loop. Repeat until the strip has 320 loops on each side (approximately 160 cm of strip length at 20 loops per 10 cm). Make two strips in the same way.
Lay the two strips side by side with inner loops facing each other. Work a
by picking up one loop from each strip alternately and working 1 double crochet through each pair. Keep tension even to avoid puckering at the join.
At each short end, thread the tails through the end loops with your tapestry needle and weave them into the central spine. Block lightly to open the loops.
